title: Canada's sport integrity watchdog introduces rules aimed at match fixing
summary: Canada’s sport integrity watchdog has created new rules aimed at discouraging competition manipulation, something its CEO describes as “a serious safety issue” for athletes.

image.caption: Sport Integrity Canada has introduced new rules aimed at discouraging competition manipulation, including match fixing. (Charles Krupa/The Associated Press file)

blocks.text: A New Game Plan
Canada’s sport integrity watchdog has created new rules aimed at discouraging competition manipulation, something its CEO describes as “a serious safety issue” for athletes.
Rules target growing safety concerns around sports betting, but aren't yet mandatory
It’s the result of growing concern around the impact of Canada legalizing single-event sports betting, according to Sport Integrity Canada CEO Jeremy Luke.

That has opened up the world of prop bets, where people can pick up their phone and gamble on everything from who will score first in an NHL game to which team in Formula 1 completes the fastest pit stops.
“What that's done is it has really increased the level of gambling that's taking place within the country and on sport,” Luke said in an interview with CBC Sports.
The risk of match fixing isn’t isolated to big-money pro leagues. According to Luke, the risk goes up in sports where athletes aren't making big salaries.
A New Game Plan: Sports Funding 101

“They can be more subject to influence or to grooming or those types of activities,” he said. “So we want to pay particular attention not just to professional sport but to lower levels of sport where that type of manipulation can occur. That's why it's really important that in Canada we have rules and education that extends across all our national sport organizations.”

The Canadian Program to Prevent Competition Manipulation prohibits athletes, sport organization staff members, board members, officials and referees, among others, from betting on any competition in their sport, regardless of the level or format. That includes directing someone to bet on their behalf.
There are also rules aimed at discouraging people from soliciting or using inside information for betting.

It bans intentional acts that could manipulate the outcome of a game, as well as acts that manipulate part of a game. Luke cited an example of a tennis player committing an intentional double fault in the third set of a second game when people have placed bets on that particular serve.

“That's the type of behaviour that we're trying to identify, but also what we're trying to do is educate athletes in particular and officials and other participants that this is a real threat to their safety,” Luke said. “Often individuals can be coerced or groomed into doing these types of things by organized crime or other individuals who are wagering on these activities.”
The rules are rolling out slowly with an initial set of voluntary adopters, as national sport organizations (NSOs) and multi-sport organizations (MSOs) review the new program.

As sport organizations sign on, Sport Integrity Canada plans to create a public registry detailing sanctions, similar to registries that already exist for those who’ve faced sanctions related to safe sport or doping violations.

blocks.text: The hope is for Sport Canada to make the rules mandatory as a condition of federal funding, similar to the safe sport and anti-doping programs administered by Sport Integrity Canada, Luke said.

“In the last couple of years, [sport organizations] have been asking for these rules to come into play as well, given they see this as a risk, and their international federations in many cases see this as a risk,” Luke said. “The reception is positive. It’s just [that] it would be far better for the rules to be mandatory in order for us to get the traction needed to get everyone to comply with the rules and to get them put into place.”
'A growing threat to the sport system'
Canadian Olympic Committee CEO David Shoemaker believes there is room in Sport Canada’s new funding framework to make it mandatory for sport organizations to adopt the new rules.

“Competition manipulation is a very important thing for us to collectively address,” Shoemaker said. “We've seen how and where it can have really negative impact on participants in sport. And we certainly support it. We fund efforts to combat it. I believe I'm about to sign on Monday the new code on behalf of the Canadian Olympic Committee and certainly wouldn't be at all disappointed to see it in there.”
It also garnered support from the Canadian Paralympic Committee. Having mandatory rules tied to funding as just a starting point, CEO Karen O'Neill said.
A New Game Plan: How high a price is pay to play sports?
“Obviously it has to have many other initiatives around to make it substantive or to have the kind of change we hope will occur, but the funding compliance framework is a first step,” she said.
The federal government acknowledges competition manipulation is a “growing threat to the sport system” that “contributes to unsafe sport environments at all levels.”
But it hasn’t yet committed to making the rules a condition of federal funding for sport organizations.

“The Government of Canada is proud to have committed funding for Sport Integrity Canada for the development and implementation of the Canadian Program to Prevent Competition Manipulation (CPPCM) and the program’s launch marks an important step in Canada’s work to address this emerging issue,” Bahoz Dara Aziz, a spokesperson for Secretary of State for Sport, Adam van Koeverden, wrote in a statement to CBC Sports.

blocks.text: “The Government of Canada will continue to monitor this issue as the CPPCM builds capacity and experience and will adjust its conditions to funded organizations to protect the integrity of sport as needed.”
Limited ability to work with law enforcement

Sport Integrity Canada initially supported the decision to remove the prohibition around single-event sports betting, seeing it as a harm reduction measure that could regulate things that were already happening on the black market.

“What didn’t follow, from our perspective, after that happened was the necessary steps to protect athletes and sport participants from this risk and to protect sport integrity more generally,” Luke said. “And that's what we've been advocating for over these years, is what goes hand-in-hand with legalization is harm reduction strategies to protect participants from these risks.”
Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There’s a push to change that

The organization would also like to see the federal government sign and ratify the Macklin Convention, which lays out a framework for how countries across the world are dealing with the issues around match fixing and sports betting.

blocks.text: Even with the new rules around match fixing, Sport Integrity Canada is missing legislation that would open the door to sharing information with law enforcement agencies that are investigating the same cases — a major gap in a world where online gambling has been used for money laundering and funding global terrorism.

“Often this is connected to organized crime,” Luke said. “You're dealing with regulators such as the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario or others. Having the ability to share information across those platforms is essential to the work that we do and it's something that we need to continue to explore.”
